Producer prices in China grew at the fastest rate since June 2022, accelerating for the third month in a row.
The PPI for October came in at 5.7%, compared to the 5.3% expected by economists polled by Reuters. The increase was driven by a sharp rise in prices in the mining and raw materials industries.
Consumer inflation in China slowed to 0.7% in October, its first deceleration after two straight months of increases.
The figure missed expectations of a 0.8% rise from economists polled by Reuters, and was lower than the 0.9% seen in September.
Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, came in at 0.8%, down from the 1% seen in the month before.
The rise in consumer prices were still held up by prices of gasoline, which was the largest contributor to the increase in prices, but this was offset by a sharper than expected fall in food prices, according to Dong Lijuan, chief statistician of the urban division at China's National Bureau of Statistics.
The Chinese economy has shown some signs of expansion recently. It grew faster than expected in the third quarter, and September saw a sharp beat in retail sales.

Since Procter & Gamble (PG -1.02%) was incorporated in 1890, the National Bureau of Economic Research has counted 26 U.S. recessions. The Panic of 1893. The Great Depression. The 1970s, twice. The dot-com bust, the financial crisis, the pandemic. Through all of it, the company that makes Tide and Pampers mailed a dividend check every single quarter, and for the last 70 years each annual check has been larger than the one before. That makes this ticker a Dividend King, a designation for companies that have increased annual dividends for at least 50 consecutive years.
All of this is not a marketing line. It is the closest thing the stock market has to a promise kept. The question for anyone buying the stock today is whether a promise that old still has something behind it.
What $10,000 in P&G stock pays today
Procter & Gamble raised its quarterly dividend to $1.0885 per share in April, a 3% increase. That works out to $4.35 a year. With the stock trading near $166, the yield is about 2.6%, so a $10,000 investment buys roughly 60 shares and produces about $265 a year in dividend income.
That is not a number that changes anyone's life. What changes a life is what the number does over time. P&G's dividend has risen more than 60% over the past decade, and if the next 10 years look like the last 10, that $260-ish becomes something north of $430 a year on the same shares, without buying another one. The point of owning P&G is not the yield you get today. It is the yield you get on the price you paid, 10 and 20 years from now, from a company that has never once broken the streak.

A 136-year dividend history is really a statement about management discipline. Every Procter & Gamble CEO since Benjamin Harrison was U.S. president has viewed the dividend as the one thing they were not allowed to touch, which forces a certain conservatism in how the company borrows, acquires, and spends. P&G's own language in the April release says it plainly: many shareholders "rely on the steady, reliable income earned with their investment in P&G."
That matters now, because things are getting harder. On its October earnings call, P&G said it expects roughly $1.4 billion in higher commodity, energy, and freight costs this fiscal year, and that oil above $100 a barrel would be an "increasing headwind." This is the operating environment in which weaker consumer companies cut their payouts; Campbell's (CPB -1.28%) and Flowers Foods (FLO -5.49%) both did this year.

Households squeezed by high grocery and gas prices are facing another hit: rising costs for home repairs and upgrades.
The cost of repairing or remodeling a home has risen steadily through October, with higher oil and energy prices, along with elevated interest rates stemming from the Iran conflict, pushing prices up. In the three months through June, it rose at the fastest quarterly pace since October 2024, according to insurance data analytics provider Verisk.
Repair bills could climb further as manufacturers of paint, plumbing fixtures, appliances and air conditioners — which already lifted prices last year due to tariffs — push through another round of increases to offset higher materials and freight costs.
“Just to put it in perspective, this quarter was the most significant inflationary period that we’ve experienced since mid-2022,” Armstrong World Industries Inc. Chief Executive Officer Mark Hershey said on an earnings call. The ceiling maker raised prices in November, noting its freight costs had risen about 20% from a year earlier.
Paint producer Sherwin-Williams Co. raised prices 8% in September and hasn’t ruled out further hikes. Pool Corp. did the same, as did HVAC manufacturer Carrier Global Corp., citing higher steel, copper, aluminum and freight costs, expecting inflationary pressures to persist into 2027.
Whirlpool Corp., which sells the KitchenAid, Maytag and inSinkErator labels alongside its namesake brand, will boost US prices by 7% in December.
“We will have meaningful inflation to address in 2027,” construction tools make Stanley Black & Decker Inc. Chief Financial Officer Patrick Hallinan said on an earnings call. “We plan to do so with productivity measures and pricing actions, with a price increase likely around the turn of the year.”
The ability to pass along higher costs to consumers depends on the product, said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Drew Reading. Homeowners are less able to avoid repairs and maintenance, though they may trade down on items like faucets or toilets.
That silver lining may put a floor under earnings. Roofing maker Carlisle Cos Inc. expects current pricing to become a tailwind as costs normalize in 2027. Price increases are expected to catch up with rising costs by the end of 2026. So far, higher prices have not hurt demand or prompted more pre-buying, CEO Christian Koch said in an earnings call.
Masco Corp., which makes faucets under brands including Hansgrohe, credited pricing with partly helping drive a 13% adjusted operating profit increase in the third quarter. Regarding potential price hikes in 2027, CEO Jonathon Nudi said pricing is the “last lever we pull.”
Existing price increases largely reflect earlier tariff and input-cost mitigation, Reading said. Accelerating copper, oil-based materials and freight costs create the potential need for Masco to raise prices in 2027.
That adds to a long-running squeeze on homeowners, with repair and remodeling costs already at a decade high, up about 64% since 2016 as of October, Verisk data shows.
Further increases are more likely to weaken demand for big-ticket discretionary items, Reading said.
Some households are already putting off larger purchases and repairing appliances rather than replacing them, according to Whirlpool CEO Marc Bitzer, though “at one point, people will replace it.”

Berkshire Hathaway Inc. spent about $9.6 billion to buy back its own shares in the third quarter, a sign the company’s executives viewed the stock as undervalued. But declining insurance underwriting weighed on its operating earnings in a mixed quarter for the company.
The Omaha, Nebraska-based conglomerate’s operating earnings fell to $12.7 billion in the third quarter, a 5.8% decline from a year earlier, it said Saturday in a statement. Insurance underwriting declined by 43%, as its auto insurer Geico faced an increase in losses and a surge in underwriting expenses over the period. The firm’s insurance net investment income also declined 14% to $2.7 billion, largely because of lower short-term interest rates.
The slump in underwriting earnings despite a lack of significant catastrophe events for Berkshire during the quarter is “a pretty significant deterioration,” said Cathy Seifert, an analyst for CFRA Research. Investors “should take a look at this because it’s a core profit generator; it’s a core float generator.”
Berkshire started buying back its own shares in the first quarter for the first time in more than a year, as Chief Executive Officer Greg Abel found the shares were trading below their “intrinsic value.”
Shares of Berkshire fell roughly 1% in the first nine months of the year, underperforming the S&P 500 — a gauge Warren Buffett often used to highlight the company’s performance. Since then, the stock has reached new heights, prompting questions over whether the firm would continue such buybacks. Its A share class has gained nearly 15% since then, versus a nearly 4% decline for the index.
Despite the buybacks, the firm’s cash pile rose from the previous quarter, totaling $377.4 billion at the end of September. After deducting $20.5 billion in unsettled US treasury bill purchases, the firm’s cash stands at about $357 billion. Berkshire sold a net $426 million of equity holdings in the period.
“Valuations of equities probably were less attractive to Abel in the third quarter,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Matthew Palazola said.
Berkshire’s earnings are typically closely watched because its stable of businesses — ranging from insurance to railroads to energy and manufacturing — provide a snapshot of the health of the US economy.

If your home isn’t in a federally designated flood zone, flooding might seem like someone else’s problem. No one requires you to buy flood insurance, and the map suggests you’re in the clear. But reality may be very different.
Mounting evidence reveals that significantly more homes are at risk of flooding than is indicated by FEMA’s 100-year flood maps – about 6 million more, and 14.6 million properties in all, by one estimate. The official maps are commonly outdated, and some are two decades old. Even when updated, they typically rely on historical flood data rather than future risk projections.
But there’s another problem that redrawing the lines won’t solve.
FEMA’s flood maps answer only one question: Is the water likely to reach my neighborhood? They don’t assess an individual home’s risks or what the impacts are likely to be when the water rises.
To understand the impact, more comprehensive data is needed, including the probable flood depth at the home, the building’s age and construction quality, and insurance coverage.
Same street, different risks
When these other factors are considered, your home’s true flood risk is far more complex than the map might seem to indicate.
The data shows how two houses on the same street can face radically different risks from flooding, even when located in the same flood zone – and where local governments can help.
One home may be newer, well maintained and covered by flood insurance. Another may be decades older, at the low end of the same street where water runs deeper during a flood, and is in poor repair and uninsured. The same storm would leave them in very different predicaments, with very different paths to recovery.
Neighborhood averages can make it hard to tell which homes are likely to be hit hardest. But understanding an individual property’s risks matters for residents figuring out how to protect a home, and for local officials deciding where limited flood-protection money should go.
We study how flooding affects homes and the people who live in them. To see how much these house-by-house differences matter, we and colleagues Aaron Flores of Arizona State University and Sara Meerow of the University of Colorado Boulder built a detailed flood risk score for nearly 1 million homes in Houston. We describe the results in a new study published in the journal Applied Geography.
Our past research in Houston found that more than half of 100,000 documented flood-prone buildings in the city currently lie outside official flood boundaries, and that these overlooked buildings are more likely to be in poor condition and uninsured, leaving them especially exposed when the floodwaters do come.
The new research helps communities locate those homes.
4 things that make a home vulnerable
To get a better understanding of each household’s vulnerability, we combined four types of information about each home.
– Water: How deep would floodwaters likely get at the home in a 100-year flood event, defined as having a 1% chance of occurrence in any given year? Here, we took a national flood model’s map of estimated parcel-level flood depths across Harris County and recorded the estimated depth at each residence.

Asphalt-roofing manufacturers have come out swinging against a new Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety standard that limits the coveted “Fortified” designation to roofs younger than 15 years. The manufacturers’ response could lend new fuel to the debate over whether insurers can or should refuse to write some aging roof systems.
The IBHS’ “sweeping conclusions are fundamentally compromised by non-standard testing protocols, unrepresentative grab-sampling, and incomplete probabilistic modeling,” the Asphalt Roofing Manufacturers Association said in recent news release. “By shifting testing procedures mid-project and omitting positive performance outcomes along with enhanced manufacturer installation guidelines, the study fails to reflect real-world roof system durability.”
The IBHS report and a technical bulletin released in September looked at IBHS’ 10-year-long study of shingles at its roof farms around the country, as well as roof examinations after three windstorm events in recent years.
The pushback over the reports comes as the Fortified designation has become the gold standard for homes built to resist high winds, with more states adopting the standard through grant-funded wind-mitigation programs or similar building codes. The IBHS, funded by the property/casualty insurance industry, reported in May that more than 100,000 structures have been designated as Fortified, with Alabama leading the way with more than half of the Fortified homes in the country. That’s double the number from 2023.
The Institute’s Sept. 29 Fortified bulletin notes that homes with roofs more than 15 years old cannot continue to win the Fortified roof designation, a certification that can lead to significant premium discounts from property insurers. The rule takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.
Institute officials could not be reached for comment, but the IBHS bulletin emphasized that the requirement applies only to Fortified home re-certification. “It does not establish asphalt shingle service life, determine whether an individual roof is fit for continued use or requires roof replacement at a particular age for any purpose other than FORTIFIED eligibility,” the bulletin reads.
Still, roofing companies worry that the IBHS reports paint too broad a brush stroke and could prompt insurers to adopt similar restrictions on any type of shingle roof, just as several Florida-based carriers did in recent years. Some of those insurers in the early 2000s—during the height of the claims litigation and assignment-of-benefits crisis in Florida—began dropping coverage for Florida homes with roofs that were older than 10 years, despite roof manufacturers’ warranties that the shingles were built to last as much as 30 years in some cases.
In 2022, Florida lawmakers responded to homeowner and roofing company complaints and enacted a law that bars insurers from non-renewing HO policies for homes with roofs less than 15 years old, solely because of the age of the roof. The law requires continuation of coverage if an inspection finds that the roof has at least five years of useful life remaining.
Only a handful of other states, including Texas and Virginia, have adopted similar governance on insurers’ renewals based solely on roof age, according to news reports and the Texas Department of Insurance.

A fire barreled through a multifamily row house in New York early Thursday, killing six people and injuring nine others, including some firefighters and police officers, the city’s fire department said.
More than 200 first responders descended on the two-story building in Brooklyn’s Sunset Park neighborhood, where Kevin Woods, the department’s chief of fire operations, said they were met with “fire on every floor.”
The severely charred building had “fire blowing out every window, meeting us at the front door,” he said at a news conference. Fire marshals were still investigating what caused the blaze.
Firefighters rescued four people, using a rear entrance to reach people trapped behind window bars, Woods said. A staircase partially collapsed inside the building, he added.
First responders brought the fire under control in about three hours, and eight people who were displaced were taken to hotels. Woods said the fire spread to one adjacent row house, but damage could be seen on buildings to both its left and right.
Row houses share common walls and exteriors and are usually built in blocks. Fire officials said the building was part of a block of 25 wood-frame homes in Sunset Park, a densely populated working-class neighborhood in southwestern Brooklyn with large Asian and Hispanic populations.
“This was a devastating fire,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at the news conference. “It will take a long time for this neighborhood to mourn the neighbors they lost this morning and to recover from this immense grief.”
The nine injured people were expected to survive, including three firefighters and two police officers who had minor injuries. No names have been released.
A lithium-ion battery was found at the scene, but it was unknown whether it was related to the fire, the department said.
Last week, an e-bike battery fire killed four people in the Bronx. It is among more than 400 fires in the city that have been linked to lithium-ion batteries this year, leading to at least six deaths and more than 70 injuries, fire officials said.
Property records show that the Brooklyn row house was erected in 1915. A family sold it a few years ago to a company called One Golden Sunshine Corp., according to city records.
Complaints filed with the city’s Department of Buildings in 2025 alleged that the basement level was illegally being converted into an apartment, and construction was underway without permits. The two apartments on the first and second floors also had been illegally divided into three units, the complaints alleged.
City inspectors visited several times — most recently in August — but were unable to gain access, according to department records. Door knocks and posted notices went unanswered, and the department ultimately closed the complaints without investigating further. It is standard protocol to close a complaint after multiple unsuccessful entry attempts, according to a 2025 city audit of the department’s enforcement actions.
Building inspectors do not have legal authority to force entry, though they can seek a warrant depending on the severity of the complaint.
Fatal home fires are not uncommon, though the death toll in the Brooklyn blaze was unusually high. A townhome fire in Chicago the same day killed four people, including a teenager.

Adobe (ADBE -2.90%) has a new Sell rating to deal with. On Nov. 4, Citigroup analyst Tyler Radke downgraded the creative software company to Sell from Neutral and cut his price target to $207 from $250. Citi sees downside risk to Wall Street's growth estimates for Adobe going into fiscal 2027.
Shares didn't drop on the news. Actually, Adobe stock gained about 1% that day.
But the stock was already having a tough year. At roughly $242 as I write, it's down about 31% in 2026.
I wrote about Adobe's long history of steep drops under two weeks ago, and Citi's Sell rating is the only new development since then. I don't think the downgrade is wrong about the direction of Adobe's growth. But I do think the stock price already bakes in something far worse than what Adobe's own numbers show.
Image source: Getty Images.
Adobe's growth is slowing
Citi points to industry data showing rising pressure on Adobe from artificial intelligence (AI) and among small businesses. It also thinks changes to the creative business under Anil Chakravarthy, who becomes Adobe's CEO on Dec. 1, might hold back short-term growth.
Adobe's own numbers already show some slowing. Heading into fiscal 2026, the company aimed for 10.2% growth in total annualized recurring revenue (ARR), a gauge of what its subscriptions pull in over a year. Later, Adobe closed its acquisition of the marketing software company Semrush, which added around $480 million in ARR. But the full-year ARR target didn't move. Without the purchase, that target comes out to growth of only around 8%.
Profits are cooling, too. Adobe's non-GAAP (adjusted) net income climbed around 8% year over year in the fiscal third quarter of 2026 (the period ended Aug. 28, 2026), down from about 11% in the fiscal second quarter and 12% in fiscal Q1. Revenue, of course, still rose 13% from a year earlier to a record $6.76 billion in fiscal Q3.
And if the slowdown in profit growth persists into fiscal 2027, Citi's concern about next year's estimates could prove right.
A higher earnings target
Earnings per share look stronger, mainly because Adobe continues to buy back its stock. Showing how much the buyback matters, the company's diluted share count shrank around 7% year over year in fiscal Q3, to 395 million. So adjusted earnings per share climbed 15% that quarter, almost twice the growth in adjusted net income.
Management has lifted its full-year earnings goal along the way, too. In December, Adobe's fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings per share target indicated growth of around 12% over fiscal 2025's $20.94. After two hikes, the latest target of $24.45 to $24.50 implies growth of around 17%.
Sure, buybacks can't hide a shrinking business forever. But Adobe isn't shrinking. Management's revenue goal for fiscal 2026 is around $26.6 billion, about 12% above the $23.8 billion Adobe took in during fiscal 2025.
Also, the company still generates billions of dollars in operating cash flow every quarter, which helps fund those buybacks. Operating cash flow was about $2.5 billion in fiscal Q3 alone.

Days after voters ousted all three Republican justices on the 15th Court of Appeals in Tuesday’s election, the court canceled oral arguments for four cases, telling lawyers the case will be reset “at a later date.”
The change will leave the cases — including a challenge to state rules limiting the sale of hemp-derived products containing THC — to three Democrats who will take office in early January.
The THC regulations, originally set to take effect at the end of March, included child-resistant packaging, a significant increase in licensing fees, new labeling, testing and bookkeeping requirements. The Texas Department of State Health Services rules also codified the legal purchasing age to 21 and increased licensing fees for manufacturers of hemp-derived THC from $258 to $10,000 per facility and retail registrations from $155 to $5,000. Industry leaders said the fees amounted to a ban by forcing businesses to close.
Smoke shops briefly pulled the products from shelves as the ban went into effect before a Travis County district judge on April 10 temporarily blocked the rules as a lawsuit by the hemp industry played out in court.
The 15th Court of Appeals, which has statewide jurisdiction over challenges to state laws and regulations, was set to hear oral arguments in the case Dec. 8.
The cancellation will let current justices deliver opinions on already argued cases, Justice Scott Field told Bloomberg Law.
“We know we can’t get the opinion out for cases orally argued before the end of the year so we don’t want to waste the lawyers’ time with an argument if there’s a chance the new court will also want to hear argument,” Field said.
There are 39 cases before the outgoing justices that have already presented oral or written arguments and are awaiting opinions.
Oral arguments set for Dec. 8 and 9 also were canceled in:
• The State of Texas vs. Sunrise Community Church Inc., a legal battle around a homeless shelter in South Austin. The attorney general’s office argued the shelter’s proximity to an elementary school makes it a public nuisance.
• Comptroller Don Huffines and Attorney General Ken Paxton vs. City of Lancaster, a dispute over about $3 million in sales taxes.
• Huffines and Paxton vs. Dave & Buster’s, which sued to recover $2.58 million that the company believed qualified for tax exemptions.

The spirit of the fall marathon is undeniably contagious: the roaring crowds, the crisp autumn air, and massive community energy. If you spectated this year, watching the hundreds (if not thousands) of runners race toward the finish line might have you yearning to lace up your shoes and hit the starting line next season. But before you jump into training, hit pause and make sure you’re prepared for success.
“Training to run a marathon will revolutionize your life, but it will also test you in brand-new ways,” says Susie Crossland-Dwyer, an avid marathoner and ultramarathoner, coach, and founder of studio s in Cincinnati. “A lot goes into a healthy, successful training season and what you do leading up to it.”
Here are nine tips that coaches want every marathoner to know to get to race day healthy, strong, and fast!
1. Make Sure You Have an Adequate Base
You’re about to set out on four-plus months of intense weekly mileage. That’s really tough on your body. To sidestep an overuse injury, having a steady foundation is crucial. A review of research on runners’ injuries published in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that the injury incidence rate among runners is 40.2 percent, and overuse from ramping up mileage or intensity too quickly causes more than 70 percent of the injuries.
“As you begin your marathon season, start with base building and don’t just jump right into doing all the miles and all the speed workouts,” advises Crossland-Dwyer, who recommends spending at least three months gradually working up to 20 to 25 miles per week before starting an official marathon training program.
2. Start Resistance Workouts
“Strength training, specifically your core and hips, is the most effective way to prevent injuries,” says Jeff Gaudette, owner and head coach at RunnersConnect. “As you ramp up your mileage for the marathon, this will be essential to you staying healthy through the training segment.”
Studies have found that strength training can also boost your performance by improving your running economy. You don’t need a certain base of strength before starting your training plan, he says, but you should include two to three weight workouts each week.
Along with weight training, “try plyometrics to get your body used to absorbing impact, single-leg exercises to prevent muscle imbalances, and mobility drills to keep your range of motion and joints healthy,” advises Meg Takacs, NASM-CPT, a run coach and founder of the Movement & Miles app.
3. Figure Out a Fueling Plan
Carb-loading before race day is what most novice runners are familiar with when starting on their marathon-training journey, but it’s only one aspect of your diet that’s important.
“Nutrition is key for successful training and a successful race—from carbs to water, electrolytes, and salt capsules,” says Takacs. “The goal is to stay ahead of any deficits before they happen because once you’re in a hydration or nutritional deficit, it’s almost impossible to come back.”
Buy water bottles to carry with you on long runs (sip water or a sports drink every 10 to 15 minutes), plus gels or gummies to nibble on every 30 minutes to stay fueled and strong through your long runs ahead.
4. Be Realistic About Training Time
We’re not talking about the race itself—though, yes, you’re going to be on your feet for a long time for that, too. But it’s important to know the kind of time commitment you’re going to be looking at for the next 16 or so weeks leading up to race day.

What is Implied Volatility?
Implied volatility shows how much movement the market is expecting in the future. Options with high levels of implied volatility suggest that investors in the underlying stocks are expecting a big move in one direction or the other. It could also mean there is an event coming up soon that may cause a big rally or a huge sell-off. Unilever supported its 24-hour moisturization claims with a short-term moisturization study (STM Study) designed to measure skin hydration over 24 hours following a single wash with Dove Deep Moisture Body Wash. NAD found that Unilever's STM Study is an appropriate study to measure moisture on the skin. Federal officials announced rural health grants to states (David DeWitt/Ohio Capital Journal).
Federal officials on Monday announced $10 billion in awards across all 50 states in the second year of the Rural Health Transformation Fund, grants created by Congress to bolster rural health in response to concerns about Medicaid cuts.
That includes $218 million for Missouri.
Texas received the largest grant for the 2027 fiscal year — almost $282 million — followed by Alaska, Montana, California and Oklahoma.
The five-year fund is providing $50 billion in grants meant to address rural healthcare access and health improvement, with $10 billion available each year until 2030.
Congress created the program in response to concern from rural health care providers — as well as lawmakers on both sides of the aisle — about the effects of sweeping Medicaid cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that President Donald Trump signed last year. Rural areas are expected to lose about $137 billion, according to health research organization, KFF.
Half of the annual funding is distributed equally among states, with each receiving $100 million in “baseline” funds. The other half is calculated based on a state’s rural population and healthcare facilities, as well as specific initiatives detailed in the applications, among other factors.
States applied for and developed their own programs, using the money toward focus areas ranging from maternal and behavioral health, preventive health and chronic disease management, access to care and the rural healthcare workforce, and tech and health equipment investments.
All 50 states submitted annual reports documenting their progress from the first year. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said it reviewed the reports as part of determining each state’s award for this year.
“States have already put these resources to work bringing better care closer to home for their rural communities, and CMS looks forward to helping them build on that progress in the coming year,” agency Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said in a news release.
States must use the grants to test out and grow approaches toward making programs sustainable after the fund’s five years have ended, the agency said.
Rural healthcare leaders have said the infusion of federal dollars is welcome but won’t be enough to offset Medicaid cuts. Goods exports soared by 35.2% last month from a year earlier, exceeding expectations for a 33.5% jump in a Reuters poll but slowing from the 36.3% growth in September.
Imports climbed by 41.6% last month, customs data showed, jumping from 31% in September and sharply beating estimates for a 32% rise by analysts polled by Reuters.

Calls from trading partners have grown louder for Beijing to boost domestic demand and balance its economy.
The strength in exports has allowed policymakers to continue relying on moderate policy support to meet the country's annual growth target of 4.5%-5%. Household consumption has remained soft, with retail sales growing a modest 1.1% in September, underscoring the imbalance in the world's second-largest economy.
Much of the surge in exports reflects robust demand for its chips and other artificial intelligence-related hardware. But any slowdown in the global AI buildout would risk denting the momentum and squeezing Chinese exporters' margins.
A separate survey by China Beige Book showed new domestic and export orders for goods slowed in October compared to a year earlier. Factory activity also unexpectedly shrank last month, according to official PMI data, as overseas orders cooled. "The stronger side of the economy got weaker," the New York-headquartered research firm said in a note on Oct. 30.
Washington and Beijing agreed in September to extend a broader trade truce by two months to January, along with a slew of other trade measures, including export-control waivers for certain critical minerals and special port fees for each other's vessels.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump are expected to meet for a third time this year at the APEC leaders' summit in Shenzhen, China next week.

At least for now, the data suggests the U.S. is gaining jobs as a result of the AI boom, not losing them.
And another category suggests the strong jobs numbers could have some staying power.

Consulting
Hiring for consultants surged in the month, sending the profession's total head count to a fresh record.
The labor force for management, scientific and technical consultants expanded by 17,300 jobs between September and October, the largest month-over-month increase in nearly two years. This category is a subset of the professional and business services sector tracked by BLS and accounted for 25% of the entire sector's gains for the month.

If history is any guide, neither of those situations will last forever. But the really important thing to understand about these two companies is that they are built to survive the entire energy cycle while still rewarding investors with dividends. Here's what you need to know.
Energy prices will eventually fall and take Exxon and Chevron with them
Exxon and Chevron are what are known as integrated energy companies. That means that they have operations across the entire energy sector, from the upstream (drilling) through the midstream (pipelines) and to the downstream (chemicals and refining). That diversification is meant to help soften the impact of commodity price swings.
That said, these two energy giants remain heavily dependent on commodity prices for their revenues and earnings. When oil prices are high, they do well; when they're low, they don't do as well and can even lose money. Energy is a commodity with a long history of volatility, rising and falling in response to supply and demand, natural and man-made disasters, and geopolitical conflicts, among other things. Right now, oil prices are high due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
History is very clear: at some point the conflict will likely end, and oil prices will decline. When that happens, Exxon and Chevron's stock prices will fall. In fact, if you are patient, the best time to buy one of these companies isn't when energy prices are high, but when they are low. Of course, that requires stepping in to buy when others are selling, which can be difficult.

Flooding on Florida’s east coast last week was so severe that it has caused the indefinite closure of a 90-bed rehabilitation hospital in Melbourne.
Sea Pines Rehabilitation Hospital, owned in part by Alabama-based Encompass Health, sustained substantial damage in the torrential rains that hammered parts of Florida’s east-central coastal areas with as much as 25 inches of rain in one day.
The 70,000-square-foot hospital was able to evacuate all patients before the floodwaters rose. Some were sent home, others went to other area hospitals.
“We are enormously grateful for the heroic efforts of our hospital staff and the first responders in ensuring the safety of our patients during this catastrophic weather event,” Pat Tuer, Encompass Health’s chief operating officer, said in a statement. “Sea Pines has served the greater Melbourne area for more than 40 years, and we are committed to restoring and enhancing our capacity to do so.”
He said that reopening Sea Pines is a high priority, but the company is discussing its options with its joint venture partner, Holmes Regional Medical Center, on the best path forward.
The hospital, on Florida Avenue in Melbourne, showed net operating revenue of $44 million for the first nine months of this year, said Encompass Health. The publicly traded company said it is the largest owner and operator of inpatient rehab hospitals in the country.
While the hospital is shut down, it will incur expenses for repairs and remediation, as well as some operating expenses. Encompass Health noted in the statement that these expenses are not indicative of the company’s overall operating performance and intends to exclude them, as well as any related insurance proceeds, from its adjusted financial results.
The three days of rain and flooding that shuttered the hospital, called a “1-in-1,000-year” event, also resulted in the deaths of two people in the area. Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for seven counties.

Matthew Martinez has lived nearly all of his 60 years in a canyon on the Navajo River and had never seen severe floods.
Then, twice over the last two weeks, the river surged through his home and outbuildings in far southwestern Colorado, about 25 miles (40 kilometers) south of the resort town of Pagosa Springs. Now a horse is missing, his barn is damaged and the river swallowed a corral. The house is strewn with mud. His tools washed downstream.
“We’re in trouble, all of us are. Not just me, everybody,” Martinez said through tears when he returned Wednesday. He said several families that go back 100 years in the same canyon had similar damage. “Nobody expected this.”
The Navajo, San Juan and Animas rivers are among those that surged beyond their banks when round after round of storms dumped heavy rain across the Four Corners region of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah.
Scientists say a supercharged El Niño event — when warm water in the Pacific disrupts weather patterns — is making heavy rainfall more likely and increasingly intense across the South.
Recent flooding has struck Flagstaff, Sedona and Tucson in Arizona; Pagosa Springs and Durango in southwestern Colorado; Farmington in northwestern New Mexico; tiny Bluff in southeastern Utah; parts of the vast Navajo Nation.
With a break in the weather at last, some evacuees are returning home.
For Martinez, who was out of town for knee surgery, getting back meant navigating a mucky mess with a four-wheel drive vehicle and a lot of patience over beaten gravel roads. And he’s finding his struggles may have just begun.
Martinez said he doesn’t have flood insurance because insurers wouldn’t provide cover for a house so near the water. He estimates at least $200,000 in losses.
He and his fiancée first stayed with one of his sons, then moved to a hotel. Both places subsequently flooded. Now they’re in an Airbnb, but he worries they could end up homeless when his emergency voucher runs out in a few days.
“The government spends, you know, just millions and billions of money on overseas and everything. Right now we need that money on this side,” he said. “We need to get this, you know, all this put back together.”
A FEMA representative came to his property and took photos after the first flood. The second flood hit three days later and was twice as bad, he said.
“I know we’re on some list right now,” Martinez said. “So we’ll listen every day and we’ll see what options we have and go from there.”
As he heals from the knee surgery, he’s considering whether he should ask family and friends for help cleaning up.
Hauling debris to the dump would cost $300 per load and ultimately could total thousands of dollars he does not readily have, he said.
The flooding did help end months of drought in the Four Corners area, but the raging torrents washed away rich topsoil on his land, leaving just sand and rock. Now he wonders how he’ll feed his remaining animals without pasture next year.
“The normal might not ever be normal again,” Martinez said.
Gruver reported from Fort Collins, Colorado.

Social media platforms face a fresh wave of European Union curbs, this time targeting addictive features and artificial intelligence chatbots.
Under a draft of the “Digital Fairness Act” seen by Bloomberg News, companies would be required to give adult users the ability to switch off features that encourage compulsive or excessive use of their services. The measures would also target AI systems that simulate personal relationships to encourage users to continue interacting with them.
The crackdown could affect some of the world’s biggest technology companies, including Meta Platforms Inc., Alphabet Inc.’s Google and ByteDance Ltd.’s TikTok, whose services rely heavily on features designed to encourage prolonged engagement. Firms would risk fines of up to 6% of worldwide annual revenue for failing to comply with the rules, set to be presented Wednesday.
The European Commission has already taken measures to rebuke social media giants for deploying features that keep users glued to their apps. Both Meta and TikTok are being investigated over suspicions of addictive design under the bloc’s content moderation rulebook, the Digital Services Act.
The EU also plans to ask social networks and AI companies to make their platforms “safe by design” as part of a sweeping Kids Act that will also restrict social media use for young teens.
The commission declined to comment on the draft of the DFA.

France has openly pointed the finger at Iran for recent cyberattacks that crippled fridges and created havoc in hundreds of supermarkets across the nation.
“The responsibility for this attack lies with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Monday in Paris, in a rare direct attribution of the hacks to a foreign power.
Barrot, who was speaking on the sidelines of an informal G7 ministerial meeting, said he would be seeking retaliatory measures against Iran and has summoned the country’s ambassador about the matter.
“This is the first large-scale cyberattack with an aim of sabotage on the national territory,” Barrot said. “It hurts the nation’s interests and the security of French citizens. We will take sanctions at the European level against all who are responsible” and “we will take any other proportionate and necessary measure to respond to this attack and dissuade those who would like to reproduce it.”
Representatives for Iran’s foreign ministry didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Related: European Supermarkets Rush to Patch Vulnerabilities After Region-Wide Fridge Hack
In parallel, Paris prosecutors said in a statement Monday they have asked an investigative judge with wider probing powers to pursue the case they’d already begun last month. They are also seeking arrest warrants against the head of an Iranian cyber unit affiliated with Iran’s IRGC and his two deputies.
Investigators identified methods for the attack that were characteristic of this offensive cyber unit, according to the prosecutors, who cited the use of Farsi and IP addresses linked to devices located in Iran.
The hacks in France, affecting some 700 supermarkets, were executed through centralized fridge controllers, connected to the internet, which allow contractors to remotely monitor temperatures. Attackers gained access to some of those systems and manipulated their settings, triggering prolonged defrost cycles that caused refrigerators and freezers to heat up.
